prompt_text: write a story from a viewpoint of a young girl that is asleep in bed and is woken up to find someone stand next to her
response_text:
I was dreaming about the big oak tree in the park, its branches swaying like the arms of a giant who was trying to hug the sky. My pillow was a cloud, my blankets a soft, warm cocoon, and I felt safe, as if the world outside my room didn’t exist at all.

Then, a sudden weight pressed against my chest, and the dream slipped away like water through my fingers. My eyes snapped open, and the darkness of my room was no longer just the night; it was something else, something alive.

For a heartbeat I lay still, my heart thudding so loudly I could hear it echo in my ears. The air smelled of the faint scent of lavender—my mom’s favorite perfume—mixed with a cool, metallic tang that I couldn’t place. My small fingers clenched the edge of the blanket, pulling it tighter around me.

There, standing at the foot of my bed, was a figure I didn’t recognize. It was tall enough that its shoulders brushed the top of my nightstand, but its shape was vague, as if the shadows themselves had taken on a form. The silhouette was dark, but not completely black; there were hints of deep blue that seemed to ripple like water in a moonlit pond.

I tried to speak, but the words got tangled in my throat. “Who…?” I managed to whisper, my voice trembling like a leaf in a windstorm.

The figure didn’t move. It didn’t speak. Instead, a soft, warm light began to spill from its chest, spreading outward in gentle waves. The light wasn’t harsh; it was the kind of glow you see when a firefly lands on a windowsill—tiny, comforting, and oddly familiar.

As the light grew, I could see more details. The figure was a girl, about my age, with hair that fell in loose curls around her shoulders. Her eyes were wide and kind, the same shade of hazel as my own, but they seemed to hold a thousand stories. She wore a simple dress that looked like it was made of moonlight and dew, and around her neck hung a tiny silver locket that caught the light and reflected it back in tiny sparks.

She lifted a hand, palm open, and placed it gently on the edge of my blanket. The moment her skin brushed the fabric, a wave of warmth rushed through me, and the fear that had been coiled in my chest began to unwind.

“Don’t be scared,” she said, her voice soft as a lullaby. “I’m not here to hurt you.”

I swallowed, feeling the lump in my throat dissolve a little. “Who are you?” I asked, my voice steadier now.

She smiled, and the smile seemed to make the room brighter, as if the shadows were retreating from a sunrise. “I’m Maya,” she said. “I used to live in this house a long time ago, when it was still new. I’m… I’m a memory. I’ve been watching over you.”

A memory? The idea felt both impossible and oddly right. I remembered hearing my grandma tell stories about a little girl named Maya who had lived in the house before I was born, about how she loved to read under the big oak tree in the park—just like the one in my dream.

“Why are you here now?” I asked, curiosity nudging the last of my fear aside.

Maya’s eyes flickered, and for a moment I thought I saw a flash of the past—a girl with a notebook, scribbling furiously under the oak’s shade, her laughter echoing through the leaves. “I’m here because you’re about to make a choice,” she whispered. “You’re scared of the new school, of the big world outside your room. I wanted to remind you that you’re never truly alone. The people who love you—your family, your friends—are always with you, even when you can’t see them.”

She reached into the locket and pulled out a tiny, silver key. It was no bigger than a grain of rice, but it glimmered with a light of its own. “Take this,” she said, pressing it into my palm. “Whenever you feel lost, hold it and remember that you have the strength to open any door.”

I felt the key’s cool metal against my skin, and a sudden surge of confidence rose within me, like the first rays of sunrise breaking through a night sky. The room seemed less dark now; the shadows receded, and the familiar shapes of my toys, my bookshelf, and the window with its curtains swaying in the night breeze came back into focus.

Maya’s form began to fade, the light from her chest dimming as if it were a candle being gently blown out. “I’ll always be here, in the corners of your heart,” she said, her voice now a whisper carried on the wind. “Sleep well, brave one.”

And then she was gone, leaving only the faint scent of lavender and the soft hum of the night. I lay there for a moment, the key warm in my hand, feeling the steady rhythm of my own breathing. The fear that had once clenched my chest was gone, replaced by a quiet excitement.

I pulled the blankets up to my chin, tucked the tiny silver key into the pocket of my pajama shirt, and let the darkness settle around me once more. This time, when I closed my eyes, I didn’t drift back to the oak tree—I drifted to a place where I knew I could be brave, because somewhere, in the quiet corners of my heart, a girl named Maya was watching, smiling, and reminding me that I could open any door I chose.

And with that thought, I fell into a deep, peaceful sleep, the night humming softly around me, as if the house itself were humming a lullaby just for me.
